So He, exalted is His majesty, said:

**In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.**

﴿By those who drag out [souls] with violence,﴾ ﴿and those who draw out gently,﴾ ﴿and those who glide along swiftly,﴾ ﴿and those who race ahead,﴾ ﴿and those who arrange the affair.﴾

This is an oath by God, exalted is He, by groups of the angels of death, peace be upon them, who draw out souls from bodies absolutely, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Or [they are the angels who draw out] the souls of the disbelievers, according to what Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Ali, may God honor his face. [The phrase] *wa-yunshituna-ha* means: they draw them out of the bodies, from *nashata al-dalw min al-bi'r* (he pulled the bucket out of the well) when he drew it out. And [they] swim in drawing them out, as one who draws out from the sea what he draws out. Thus they race and hasten with the souls of the disbelievers to the Fire and with the souls of the believers to Paradise. Then they arrange the matter of their punishment and reward, by preparing them to perceive what has been prepared for them of pains and pleasures.

Some scholars inclined to restrict *al-nazc* (drawing out with force) to the souls of the disbelievers, and *al-nashat* and *al-sabh* (gliding) to the souls of the believers. This is because *al-nazc* is a pulling with intensity, and it has been followed by the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿gharqan﴾ (with violence). It is an emphatic verbal noun with its extra letters dropped, meaning: drawing out with great intensity from the furthest parts of the bodies. It was also said: [*al-nazi'at*] is a type, and *al-nazc* is a genus, i.e., in this context, and that is more fitting for the disbelievers.

Ibn Mas'ud said: The angels draw out the soul of the disbeliever from his body from beneath every hair, from beneath the nails, and from the roots of the feet. Then they plunge it into his body, then draw it out until it nearly emerges, then return it into his body, and so on repeatedly. This is their work with the disbelievers. *Al-nashat* is drawing out gently and easily, and it is more fitting for the believers. Likewise *al-sabh* clearly indicates moving gently and softly. One of the early scholars said: The angels draw the souls of the believers out with a gentle drawing, then leave them until they rest a little, then draw them out gently and softly, like one who swims in water, who moves gently so as not to drown. So they act gently in that extraction, so that no pain or severity reaches the believer.

In *al-Taj* (*Taj al-'Arus*) it is said that *al-nashat* is untying a knot gently. It is said, as in *al-Bahr*: *ansha'tu al-'iqal* and *nashsha'tuhu* when you pull its *unshuwah* (slipknot) and it comes loose. The *unshuwah* is a knot that is easily loosened when pulled, like the knot of a belt. If you make *al-nazi'at* the angels of punishment and *al-nashitat* the angels of mercy, the conjunction [*wa*] would be for difference in essence, as is the original usage. The *fa* (then) in the last two indicates that they follow what precedes them without delay. The accusative of *nashtan*, *sabhan* and *sabqan* is as a verbal noun, like the accusative of *gharqan*. As for the accusative of *amran*, it is as an object of *al-mudabbirat* (those who arrange), not by removing the preposition; i.e., by a command from Him, exalted is He, as it has been said. It was claimed that this is preferable. Its indefiniteness is for awe and grandeur. It is also permissible that *gharqan* be a verbal noun interpreted as an adjective, its accusative being also as an object for *al-nazi'at*, or an adjective of the object of it; i.e., souls sunk into the bodies.

This includes the angels of mercy and the angels of punishment, and the conjunction with it is for difference of the described as well as of the attributes. Whatever the case,

Some restricted this to five of the saints. All of this is ignorance, though the second is greater ignorance. Yes, there is no reason to hesitate that God, exalted is He, may honor whom He wills of His saints after death, as He honors them before it with what He wills. So He, glorified is He, cures the sick, rescues the drowning, grants victory over the enemy, sends down rain, and such and such, as an honor to him. Perhaps He, mighty and majestic is He, may show someone resembling him in form, and he does what God, exalted is He, was asked by his sanctity regarding matters with no sin in them, in response to the petitioner. Perhaps the request is made in a manner forbidden by law, and then He, glorified is He, displays something similar as a trick against the petitioner and as a gradual leading on. I did not find anything that confirms its soundness in the Book, the Sunnah, or the statements of the early generations of the Ummah. The Imam himself, in al-Mabahith al-Mashriqiyya, mentioned the impossibility of more than one soul being attached to a single body, and likewise the impossibility of a single soul being attached to more than one body. He did not follow up on what he related here, so it seems he understood that the attachment meant here is other than the impossible attachment. So do not be heedless. He said, regarding the interpretation of the things mentioned as referring to the angels, that the angels, peace be upon them, have negative attributes and relational attributes. As for the first, they are free from desire, anger, blameworthy character traits, death, old age, sickness, composition, organs, humours, and elements; rather, they are spiritual substances free from these conditions. "Al-nazi'at gharqa" (By those who pull out violently) is an indication of their being removed from these conditions with a complete removal in all respects, given that the form (of the word) is for attribution. "Wal-nashitat nashta" (And those who glide along smoothly) is an indication that their departure from that is not like the departure of humans, which is by way of hardship and difficulty, but rather in accordance with their quiddity. So the two words are indications defining their negative conditions. As for their relational attributes, they are of two kinds. The first explains their rational faculty and clarifies their state in knowing the dominion of God, Exalted is He, and His kingdom, glorified is He, and in perceiving the light of His majesty, majestic is His majesty. So He, glorified is He, described them in this context with two descriptions: one of them is "Wal-sabihat sabha" (And those who swim swiftly), for they swim from the beginning of their nature in the seas of His majesty, Exalted is He; then there is no end to their swimming, because there is no end to the greatness of God, Exalted is He, the exaltedness of His self-sufficiency, the light of His majesty and His grandeur, so they are forever in that swimming. The second is "Fal-sabiqat sabqa" (And those who race forward in a race), which indicates the difference of their ranks in degrees of knowledge and in levels of manifestation. The second kind explains their active faculty and clarifies their state in it, so He, glorified is He, described them in this context with His saying, Exalted is He: "Fal-mudabbirat amra" (And those who arrange the affair). Since arranging cannot be completed except after knowledge, He placed the explanation of the rational faculty before the explanation of the active faculty." End of quotation. Although some of it is open to objection, it is not closely suited to the context. More than one scholar has transmitted opinions other than what was mentioned regarding the interpretation of these things. From Mujahid: "al-nazi'at" are the deaths that pull out souls. Yahya ibn Salam related that they are wild beasts that move toward pasture. From the first (Mujahid) also, "al-nashitat" is interpreted as deaths too. From Ata', it is interpreted as wild cows and similar animals that move energetically from one region to another. From him also, "al-sabihat" is interpreted as ships. From Mujahid, it is interpreted as deaths swimming into the souls of animals. From some, it is interpreted as clouds, and from another as sea creatures. From some, "al-sabiqat" is interpreted as deaths, in the sense that they outrun hopes. From more than one, "al-mudabbirat" is interpreted as: Jibril, who arranges the winds, the armies, and revelation; Mikail, who arranges rain and plants; Izra'il, who arranges the taking of souls; and Israfil, who arranges the command descending upon them, because it descends with him, and who arranges the blowing into the Trumpet. Most scholars interpret them as angels in general. Indeed, Ibn Atiyya said: "I do not know of any disagreement that they are the angels," and, as far as I know, there is no sound report from the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, concerning the interpretation of any of what has been mentioned. What I mentioned first is the preferred view in my opinion, based on the context. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 6:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿On the Day when the Quaker quakes﴾ is in the accusative case, governed by an implied response (jawab, the consequent clause of the oath). By "the Quaker" (al-Rajifah) is meant either the Event (al-Waqi'ah) or the Blast (al-Nafkhah) by which bodies quake. The ascription of the quaking to it is then metaphorical (majazi), since it is the cause of the quaking; or the figure lies in the attribution, by making the cause of the quaking itself the one that quakes. It is also permissible to interpret al-Rajifah as "the Agitator" (al-Muharrikah), in which case the ascription is literal (haqiqah), because rajafa (to quake) can mean harraka (to set in motion) and taharraka (to move), as stated in the Qamus (al-Qamus al-Muhit, the lexicon). This is the First Blast (al-Nafkhah al-Ula). It has also been said that what is meant is the motionless bodies whose movement becomes intense at that time, such as the earth and the mountains, in support of the Exalted's saying: ﴿On the Day when the earth and the mountains quake﴾. Calling them "quaking" (rajifah) is by consideration of their first state, so there is in this an metonymy of the sort called majaz mursal (figurative usage by a loose relation), and by this the purpose of the ascription becomes clear.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 7:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Followed by the Radifah (the second blast)﴾. That is, the Wa'iyah (the one that sits firmly, i.e., the impact), or the blast that follows and comes after the first, which is the second blast. It has also been said: the following bodies, namely the sky and the stars, for they will be split and scattered afterward. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿the Rajifah﴾, justifying the placing of the Day as a time-frame (zarf) for the Resurrection, because it conveys the extension and breadth of the time, since it conveys that the Day is the time of the quaking, which is restricted by its being followed by the Radifah. The following of one thing by another is a branch of the existence of that first thing, so there must be an extension of the Day up to the Radifah, and its extension is taken into account, even though the Resurrection does not occur at the Radifah, meaning the second blast. Between it and the first there are forty (years), to magnify the Day by explaining that it is the occasion of two great calamities. It has also been said: "The Day when the earth quakes" (yawma tarjufu) is in the accusative governed by "remember" (udhkur), so the clause will be a resumptive statement confirming the content of the implied answer, as if it were said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Remember for them the Day of the two blasts, for it is the time of their resurrection." It has also been said: it is in the accusative governed by what indicates it.

"His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Hearts that Day will be trembling﴾. That is, on the day the hearts quake (wajifat), i.e., are agitated. It is said: the heart throbbed (wajafa al-qalbu wajifan), meaning it pounded from intense terror; similarly, it throbbed (wajaba wajiban). It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that wajifah means khA'ifah (fearful) in the dialect of Hamdan. And from al-Suddi: "departing from its place." The word wajifah was not made a nasb (accusative) governed by "wajifah," because it has already put in the accusative its adverbial complement, namely "yawma'idhin" (that Day). Establishing a meaning (ta'sis) is better than emphasis (ta'kid), so it should not be read as emphasis; moreover, the omission of the modified noun (hadhf al-mudaf) and the substitution of tanwin are also things that reject this reading.

﴿Hearts﴾ is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), ﴿that Day﴾ is attached to ﴿trembling﴾, and ﴿trembling﴾ is the predicate (khabar), according to what has been said, and this is the most apparent view, as in His saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾, ﴿looking toward their Lord﴾, and ﴿faces that Day will be gloomy﴾. It is permissible to begin with an indefinite noun (nakirah) because its indefiniteness is for classification (li'l-tanwi'), and this stands in the place of a qualifying descriptor that specifies it. Indeed, classification is more apparent in the parallel instance, due to the mention of the opposite, unlike what we are dealing with here; but there is no difference once the meaning has been directed toward it. If you wish, you may consider it as indicating multiplicity (lil-takthir), as it was considered in: "An evil that bares the fanged one" (sharr aharra dha nabin). And it has been said: ﴿trembling﴾ is an adjective (sifah) of ﴿hearts﴾, which justifies beginning with it."

The Almighty's words: ﴿Their eyes will be humbled﴾ means that the eyes of its people will be abased from fear, and for this reason it was annexed to them (ʾidafa, the grammatical annexation, is used here because of the closest connection). It is also permitted that by "eyes" is meant the insights (baṣāʾir), i.e., the insights will become abased and will not perceive anything. He used their abasement as a metonym for their failure to perceive, because the honour of insight lies only in perception. It has been examined whether hearts will not perceive on the Day of Resurrection, and the answer is that what is meant is intense bewilderment and confusion. The phrase is a nominal sentence (jumla min mubtadaʾ wa khabar) in the place of raising as a predicate (khabar) for "hearts."

It has been objected that it is well known that the descriptive adjective (ṣifa) must be known to the listener as belonging to the thing described, to the point that more than one scholar said: adjectives before knowledge of them are predicates, and predicates after knowledge of them are adjectives. Since the occurrence of trembling and the occurrence of humility are equal for the eyes of the people of the hearts, in knowledge and in ignorance alike, making the first the topic of the subject, established and taken for granted, and making the second the thing reported, intended for the benefit, is a purely arbitrary decision. Moreover, trembling, which is an expression for the agitation and anxiety of the heart from intense fear and dread, is more severe and more terrifying than the humility of the sight. So the more terrifying of the two evils was made the main element, and the less severe was made the secondary element, which is not familiar in speech. Also, restricting humility to hearts described by a specific attribute, one that does not imply generality and comprehensiveness, is a belittling of the matter in a context that calls for magnification. End of quotation.

Page 27

You know that what is well known and what more than one scholar said is not agreed to be universally applicable, and that some of what was objected to is refuted according to what the words of some eminent scholars imply, namely that it is permissible to make the singular noun a predicate with the clause following it being a descriptive adjective. But this is far-fetched. As for what was said regarding the first view, that making the nunation (tanwīn) one of classification (tanwīʿ) while attaching it is contrary to the apparent meaning, and that its being like an adjective in meaning is an arbitrary departure from fairness, Ibn ʿAṭiyya claimed that the indefinite noun was specified by the words of the Almighty: ﴿that Day﴾. It has been objected that it is not specified by times and adverbs of time in relation to bodies. Isam al-Din estimated the answer to the oath as: ﴿they will surely come﴾. He said: We estimate it this way, and we make "the Day the quaking will quake" a subject with a nominative position, and we make ﴿the following one will follow it﴾ a descriptive adjective (ṣifa) of "the quaking," by treating it as in the position of the indefinite, because the definiteness is for the mental (dhihnī) reference, like the saying: "I pass by the base man who insults me." But in this there is what there is. It was also said that the answer is ﴿the following one will follow it﴾, and "the Day" is in the accusative governed by it, and the particle of the oath is omitted, meaning: "for a day such as this, the following one will follow it." The nūn of emphasis did not enter, because the estimated particle was separated from the verb. But this is not right. Muhammad ibn ʿAli al-Tirmidhi said that the answer to the oath is: ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾, and that is as you see. Similar to it is what was said: it is ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾, because it is in the estimate of "Indeed it has reached you." Abu Hatim said, with transposition and inversion, as if it were said: ﴿then they will be upon the earth awake﴾ (al-Nazi'at), and Ibn al-Anbari criticised him, saying that the particle fa' (then) is not used to begin speech. In sum, the most suitable view is the one we presented earlier.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 10:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They say, "Shall we indeed be restored to our former state?"﴾ This is a report of what those who deny the Resurrection say, those who reject the verses that speak of it, after the affirmation of its occurrence by way of an oath, and after the mention of its terrifying preliminaries and what befalls hearts and eyes when they occur. That is: when it is said to them, "You will be resurrected," they say, denying it and marvelling at it: ﴿Shall we indeed be returned﴾ after our death ﴿to our former state (al-hafirah)?﴾ That is, to the first condition, meaning life, as Ibn 'Abbas and others said. It has also been said that when He, exalted is His majesty, swore an oath concerning the Resurrection and made clear their humiliation and fear, He mentioned here their acknowledgment of the Resurrection and their return to life after death. Accordingly, the interrogative is for expressing astonishment at what they witnessed after their denial, and the sentence is a resumptive sentence of explanation (isti'naf bayani) for what they say at that time. The apparent meaning is what preceded, and that the saying is in this world. In any case, it derives from their saying: "So-and-so returned along his hafirah," meaning along his path by which he came and which he dug; that is, he left an impression on it by his walking. The regular form would be "al-mahfurah" (the dug one), so it is either in the sense of "possessing digging," or the attribution is metaphorical, or the expression is a metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah) by likening the receptive to the agent and making hafiriyyah a figurative imagining. This is similar to what they mentioned regarding ﴿a pleasing life﴾. It is said of everyone who was in a matter, then left it and then returned to it: "He returned to his hafirah." Upon this is the saying of the poet:

Hafirah, upon baldness and grey hair? God forbid from folly and shame.

He means: Shall I return to what I was upon in my youth of amorous pursuits and youthful vanity, after I have grown grey? God forbid that from me, as folly and shame.

From it is the proverb: "The payment is at the hafirah." It has been said that hafirah in it means the first condition, which is the bargain, that is, payment at the time of the contract. However, al-Maydani transmitted from Tha'lab that its meaning is payment at the race, for when a horse wins it takes the stake. Al-Hafirah is the ground which the leader dug with its hooves, according to one of the interpretations. It has also been said that "al-hafirah" is the plural of al-hafir in the sense of the foot, meaning ﴿They say, "Shall we indeed be returned"﴾ alive, walking on our feet and treading the earth with them. It is not hidden that the expression bearing this meaning is not apparent. From Mujahid: "al-hafirah" means the dug graves, that is, "Shall we indeed be returned alive in our graves." From Zayd ibn Aslam: it is the Fire, and this, as you see, is far-fetched. Abu Haywah, Abu Bahriyyah and Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited "fi al-hafirah" with a fatha on the ha' and a kasra on the fa', as an adjectival form (sifah mushabbahah) from hafira, the intransitive, like 'alima, the passive counterpart of huffira (in the passive voice). It is said: "His teeth decayed (hafirat asnanuhu), so they became hafar (decayed) with two fathas," when the eating-away affects the teeth and they change. This returns to the meaning of "the dug one." It has also been said that it is the foul-smelling land changed by the bodies of its dead.

And His saying, ﴿Even when we are bones, decayed?﴾ is an emphasis on their denial of resurrection, by mentioning a state that contradicts it. The governing element for "idha" (when) is an implied verb indicated by "mardudun" (we will be returned): meaning, "When we are decayed bones, will we be returned and resurrected, even though that is the furthest thing from life?"

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "idha kunna" without the interrogative hamza. It was said that this is a statement of mockery following the interrogative of denial. It has been deemed more likely that it is connected to "mardudun."

'Umar, Ubayy, 'Abdullah, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn 'Abbas, Masruq, Mujahid, al-Akhawan (the two brothers), and Abu Bakr read "nakhiratan" with an alif (ناخِرَةً). It is like "nakhiratin" (نَخِرَةٍ), from "nakhara al-'azmu" (the bone decayed), meaning it became decayed and hollow, so that the wind passes through it and a "nakhir" (a sound, a whistling) is heard from it. The recitation of the majority is more eloquent. They have explicitly stated that "fa'il" (فَعِلًا) is more eloquent than "fa'il" (فاعِلٍ), even though its letters are more numerous. Their saying "an increase in the structure indicates an increase in meaning" holds generally, or when the category is the same, not when it differs, such as when "fa'il" is an active participle (ism fa'il) and "fa'il" (فَعِلٌ) is an attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah). Yes, that recitation better suits the ends of verses (ra'us al-ayy), and choosing it for that reason does not imply that the two are equal in emphasis, as some have wrongly thought. The majority held the view of greater eloquence, and "nakhirah" was interpreted accordingly as "most decayed." 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "al-nakhirah" is the one that has already decayed, and "al-nakhirah" (ناخِرَةُ) is the one that has not yet decayed. The equivalence of meaning has been reported from al-Farra', Abu 'Ubaydah, Abu Hatim, and others.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 12:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said﴾, narrating another disbelief of theirs, branching out from their earlier disbelief. Perhaps the placing of "they said" between the two is to indicate that the emission of this disbelief from them is not in the manner of constancy and continuity, unlike their earlier disbelief, whose emission from them is continuous at all their times, as is indicated by its narration in the present tense (muḍāriʿ). That is: they said, mockingly, pointing to what they denied of the return to the "ḥāfirah" (the original state of life), implying the extreme remoteness of its occurrence: ﴿That, then, would be a losing return﴾; that is, possessing loss, or its people being losers. That is: if that return is true, then we are losers for denying it. And they presented what they were certain of its non-existence and impossibility in the form of what is likely to occur, for greater mockery. Al-Hasan said: ﴿losing﴾ means false, i.e., not occurring. The meaning would then be: that return, if we were decayed bones, is not going to happen.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 13:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is but one shout﴾, is an explanation (ta'lil) of an implied premise (muqaddar) that their denial of that requires; for since the crux of the matter was their finding the return (al-karrah) difficult, He answered them concerning that, and it was said: Do not consider that return difficult; for it is but one shout, that is, it is accomplished by one shout, which is the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thaniyah). He expressed it by the shout (sayhah) to draw attention to the complete connectedness of the blast with the shout, as if the two were one and the same. It was also said: the pronoun "hiya" refers back to al-radifah (the Following Event).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 14:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then they will be in the sahirah (the wakeful, or open, ground)﴾. Here, "then" (idha) (hina'idhin) explains that the return follows the single shout (zajrah) suddenly; that is, "then they will be alive upon the surface of the earth, after they had been dead in its belly." And according to the first view, it explains their presence at the place of standing (mawqif) immediately after the return, which He expressed by the zajrah.

As for al-Sahirah, it is said: it is the surface of the earth and the open wasteland (falah). They recited the verse of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

In it is the flesh of a sahirah and a sea, and what they utter will never cease to abide.

In al-Kashshaf: it is the white earth, that is, the one without vegetation, level. It was named so because the mirage (sarab) flows over it, from their saying: "a sahirah spring" meaning a spring whose water flows, and its opposite is "na'imah" (sleeping). Al-Ash'ath ibn Qays said:

And a sahirah over which the mirage rises, covering its regions; I have crossed it, veiled.

Or it is named so because whoever travels it does not sleep, for fear of perishing. According to the first explanation, it is a metaphor upon a metaphor; according to the second, "sahar" (wakefulness) is in its literal sense and the figurative usage lies in the attribution.

Al-Raghib related two opinions concerning it: the first, that it is the surface of the earth; the second, that it is the earth of the Resurrection. Then he said: its real meaning is that upon which treading is frequent, so it is as though it has stayed awake from that, alluding to what the poet said:

The earth's awake one stirs, and so does its sleeper.

Al-Dahhak related from Ibn Abbas that al-Sahirah is an earth of silver upon which Allah, Exalted is He, was never disobeyed; He creates it at that time. And from him also: it is the earth of Makkah. It is also said: it is the seventh earth, which Allah, Exalted is He, will bring forth, and upon it He will call the creatures to account; this will be when the earth is changed into another earth. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: it is a mountain in Syria which Allah, Exalted is He, will extend on the Day of Resurrection for the gathering of people. Abu al-'Aliyah and Sufyan said: it is an earth near Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It is also said: al-Sahirah means the open plain upon the edge of Hell. Qatadah said: it is Hell itself, because no one within it sleeps.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 15:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Has the story of Musa come to you?﴾ is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), sent down to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the denial of his people and their threats against him, namely that there would befall them the like of what befell those who were stronger than them and greater. The meaning of ﴿Has it come to you?﴾ is that it is taken as a consideration that this is the first time the story of Musa (peace be upon him) reached him, (peace be upon him) [i.e., the Prophet (ﷺ)].

It is an encouragement for him (ﷺ) to listen to his story, as if it were said: "Has the story of Musa come to you? I will inform you of it." And if its coming is taken to be before this, which is what is most evident from the brevity in the narration, then it means: "Has not his story already come to you?" Yet *hal* here does not carry the meaning of *qad* in either of the two aspects.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa﴾ is an adverbial clause (zarf) governing "the narration" (al-hadith), not "the coming" (al-ityan), because their two times differ. It has also been permitted that it be the object of an implied "remember" (udhkur), so that it reads as "remember when...".

The discussion of "the sacred valley" has already been given, and there is difference among the readers (qurra') regarding "Tuwa". The clause ﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾ is taken as implying the verb "say" (al-qawl), so the estimated sense is: "and He said to him," or "saying to him".

﴿Go﴾ etc.

It was said: it is an explanation of the call, meaning: He called to him, "Go." It was also said: it is with the omission of the explanatory "an" (that), which is indicated by the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud): "an idhhab" (that go), because in the call there is the meaning of saying. It is also permissible that it be with the implied masdariyyah (the particle that turns the following verb into a verbal noun) preceded by a prepositional particle [i.e., bi-an idhhab, "with [the sense of] going"]. ﴿Indeed he has transgressed.﴾ This is a reason given for the command, or for the obligation to obey it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 18:

﴿So say﴾ after you have come to him, ﴿"Would you like to purify yourself"﴾ That is: Is there in you an inclination to purify yourself? Thus ﴿لَكَ﴾ (laka, "for you") is in the position of the predicate of an omitted subject, and ﴿إلى أنْ تَزَكّى﴾ (ila an tazakka, "to purify yourself") is connected to that omitted subject. A similar usage is the words of the poet:

فَهَلْ لَكم فِيها إلَيَّ فَإنَّنِي بَصِيرٌ بِما أعْيا النِّطاسِيَّ حِذْيَما

It is said: "Hal laka fi kadha?" (Is there for you in such-and-such?), where the particle fi is used, and the subject is understood to be "raghbah" (desire). Similarly, what is transitive with it. Some have estimated the subject here as "raghbah" too, because it is also transitive with it. Abu al-Baqa' said: Since the meaning is "I invite you," ila is brought in; perhaps he made the adverbial phrase connected to the sense of the statement, or to an omitted element that indicates it. ﴿تَزَكّى﴾ (tazakka) is with one of the two tas elided, meaning: you purify yourself from the filth of disbelief and transgression. The two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') and Abu 'Amr, in one transmission, read "tazzakka" with the zay doubled, and its original form, as we have indicated, is "tatazakka," where the second ta was assimilated into the zay.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 19:

﴿And I would guide you to your Lord, so you would fear [Him].﴾ That is: I would direct you to knowing Him, glory be to Him and exalted is He, so that you would know Him, ﴿so you would fear [Him]﴾, since fear (khashyah) does not occur except after knowing Him. God Most High says: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ [35:28]. He made fear the goal of guidance, because it is the essence of the matter (milak al-amr): whoever fears God Most High, every good comes from him, and whoever feels secure becomes bold toward every evil. Among this is the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as related by al-Tirmidhi from Abu Hurairah: "Whoever fears travels by night, and whoever travels by night reaches the destination."

In the interrogative form there is, as is not hidden, gentleness in the call and in bringing down [the tyrant] from his arrogance. This is a detailed explanation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he will be reminded or fear﴾ [20:44]. And placing purification (tazkiyah) before guidance (hidayah) is because purification is clearing away (takhliyah).

The fa' in His words ﴿So he showed him the greatest sign﴾ is an explanatory fa' (fa' fasiha), which reveals clauses that have been omitted because their detail is given elsewhere. It is as if it were said: he went and such-and-such happened, and then he showed him. Al-Zamakhshari, in his marginal glosses (al-Hawashi) on his commentary, limited himself to supposing one omitted clause. He said: this is conjoined to something omitted, and the meaning is: he went and then showed him, because His words ﴿Go﴾ indicate it. It is like ﴿Strike the rock with your staff, and there gushed forth from it﴾.

The showing (ira'a) may mean causing to know (ta'rif), for the accursed one, when he saw them, recognized them. His claim that they were sorcery was only a display of defiance. Attributing them to him (peace be upon him) is in terms of outward appearance, just as attributing them to the plural of majesty (nun al-'azama) in His words ﴿And We had certainly shown him Our signs﴾ is in terms of reality.

By the greatest sign, according to what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, is the turning of the staff into a serpent, since it was the initial and principal one, and the other was secondary to it. According to what is related from Mujahid, it is that and the white hand, since the two are, in terms of indication, like a single sign. He expressed them in the plural form in His words ﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs﴾, in consideration of the wondrous matters contained within them, each of which is a clear sign for a people who reason.

It is also permissible that it means the totality of his miracles (peace be upon him), with the singular form being in consideration of what was mentioned. The fa' then denotes the immediate sequence of its first part, or the totality with consideration of its first part. Its being "greatest" is in consideration of the miracles of earlier messengers (peace be upon them), or the fa' is for absolute addition. Its remoteness is not hidden. What makes it more remote is the ordering of the gathering of the sorcery afterward, for that did not happen except upon the showing of those two signs, and his turning away from acting in accordance with their requirement. As for the other nine, they appeared at his hand (peace be upon him) only after the sorcerers had been overcome, gradually, over a period of about twenty years.

The extremist Shi'a (ghulat al-Shi'a) claimed that the greatest sign was 'Ali (may God ennoble his face), that He showed him it while his noble spirit was being transformed into its most exalted state. This is raving beyond the bounds of reason and beyond the bounds of transmitted report.

[p. 30]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 21:

﴿Then he denied﴾ Moses, peace be upon him, and called his miracle sorcery. ﴿And disobeyed﴾ God, exalted is He, by rebelling after he knew the truth of the command and the obligation of obedience, with the most severe and most ugly disobedience, in that he dared to deny the existence of the Lord of the worlds altogether. The accursed one and his people were commanded to worship Him, mighty and majestic is He, and to abandon the greatness that the tyrant claimed and that his rebellious group accepted from him, not merely to send the Children of Israel out of bondage and coercion. In making the object of the denial Moses, peace be upon him, and the object of the disobedience God, mighty and majestic is He, there is something that is not present in making both of them Moses, as it has been said: "Then Moses denied his staff," which carries blame, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 22:

﴿Then he turned his back﴾ he turned away from obedience. ﴿Striving﴾, i.e., striving diligently to nullify his command (peace be upon him) and to oppose the sign. And "then" (thumma) is used because nullifying that and undoing it requires a long time. It is also permissible that the turning back is in its literal sense, i.e., "then he departed from the assembly, striving to nullify that." It has also been said: he turned his back, striving, fleeing from the serpent. For it is narrated that when he cast down the staff, it turned into a serpent, enormous, its mouth wide open, between its jaws eighty cubits; so it placed its lower jaw on the ground and its upper jaw on the wall of the palace. Pharaoh fled, defecated, and the people fled in a crush, and twenty-five thousand of his people died. In some traditions it is said that it turned into a snake, rose into the sky a distance of a mile, then descended, approaching Pharaoh, and began saying: "O Musa, command me with whatever you wish." Pharaoh said: "I implore you by the One who sent you, take it!" So he took it, and it returned to being a staff. And you know that if this was after the gathering of the magicians for the contest, as is well known, then the intended meaning here does not appear correct if "the gathering" is meant as their gathering after which this occurred; and if it was after the denial and disobedience but before the gathering, then its delay relative to the first two does not appear. Yes, it has been said that "then" in this case serves to indicate the improbability of his turning back in terror and haste while claiming divinity. It has also been said that what is meant by His words, glorified is He, "Then he turned his back," is "then he came forward and acted"; i.e., he initiated, but the turning back was placed in the position of the coming forward, as an allusion and a warning that for him it was destruction and reversal.

﴿So he gathered [his people] and called out﴾: that is, he gathered the magicians, in accordance with His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Then Pharaoh sent into the cities to gather [the magicians]﴾. And His saying, glorified be He: ﴿Then Pharaoh turned away, and gathered his plotting, then came back﴾; that is, what he plotted with of the magicians and their instruments. It has also been said: he gathered his soldiers, and it is permissible that what is meant is that he gathered the people of his kingdom.

﴿And called out﴾ in that very assembly itself, or through the agency of a herald. The first view is supported by His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And said, "I am your lord, the Most High"﴾. On the second view there is an ellipsis in it; that is: "and said: Pharaoh says, 'I am your lord'" and so on, along with the figurative usage found in the second view. In some reports it is related that he stood among them as a preacher and said that great utterance, and the accursed one intended to elevate himself above everyone who manages their affairs.

﴿So he gathered [his people] and called out﴾: that is, he gathered the magicians, in accordance with His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Then Pharaoh sent into the cities to gather [the magicians]﴾. And His saying, glorified be He: ﴿Then Pharaoh turned away, and gathered his plotting, then came back﴾; that is, what he plotted with of the magicians and their instruments. It has also been said: he gathered his soldiers, and it is permissible that what is meant is that he gathered the people of his kingdom.

﴿And called out﴾ in that very assembly itself, or through the agency of a herald. The first view is supported by His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And said, "I am your lord, the Most High"﴾. On the second view there is an ellipsis in it; that is: "and said: Pharaoh says, 'I am your lord'" and so on, along with the figurative usage found in the second view. In some reports it is related that he stood among them as a preacher and said that great utterance, and the accursed one intended to elevate himself above everyone who manages their affairs.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 25:**

﴿So Allah seized him, as a punishment (nakal) for the Hereafter and the former life.﴾ *Nakal* (punishment, exemplary chastisement) is used in the sense of *tankil* (making an example of someone), as *salam* is used in the sense of *taslim* (greeting). It is the punishment that deters whoever sees or hears of it and prevents him from engaging in what leads to it. It is in the accusative because it is an emphatic verbal noun (*masdar mu'akkid*), like *wa'da Allah* (ﷻ) and *ṣibghata Allah* (ﷻ) [in the Qur'an]. It is as if it were said: "Allah made an example of him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the former life," which is burning in the Hereafter and drowning and humiliation in this world.

It is also permitted that it be in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) of *akhadha* (seized), i.e., "Allah seized him with the seizing of the punishment of the Hereafter..." etc. And that it be an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), i.e., "He seized him for the sake of a punishment," etc. And that it be in the accusative by the removal of the preposition (*naz' al-khafid*), i.e., "He seized him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the former life." Its being attributed to the two abodes is based on the seizing itself occurring in them, not on the basis that the meaning of deterrence contained in it occurs in them, for that is not conceivable in the Hereafter but only in this world. For the punishment of the Hereafter deters whoever hears of it, and prevents him from engaging in what leads to it, in this world.

It is also permitted that it be in the sense of a derived noun (*mushtaqq*) as a circumstantial state (*hal*), and its attribution is in the sense of *fi* (in): i.e., "making an example for whoever sees or hears of him in the Hereafter and the former life." It is also permitted that the attribution be in the sense of *li* (for). Taking "the Hereafter and the former life" to mean the two abodes is the apparent meaning, and it is narrated from al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and others. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrimah, al-Dahhak and al-Sha'bi that "the Hereafter" refers to his saying: ﴿I am your Lord, the Most High﴾, and "the former life" refers to his saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾. It has also been said the reverse, so they are two utterances.

Page 31

Between them, according to what they said, was a period of forty years. Abu Razin said: "The former" is the state of his disbelief and rebellion, and "the Hereafter" is his saying: ﴿I am your Lord, the Most High﴾. And from Mujahid: they are two expressions for the first and last of his sins; i.e., he was made an example of for all of them. The attribution in all of these is an attribution of the cause to the effect (*idafat al-musabbab ila al-sabab*). The position of whoever holds that Pharaoh's faith was accepted leads to these statements, and that punishment was taken to be the drowning in this world. We have already discussed this matter earlier.

Indeed in that (ʾinna fī dhālika) means: in what has been mentioned of the story of Pharaoh, what he did, and what was done to him. "Surely there is in that a lesson" (laʿibratan), a great one, "for whoever fears" (li-man yakhshā), meaning: for whoever is of such a disposition that he fears, and he is one for whom knowledge is part of his nature. This is either because one who is already in fear does not need to take a lesson, or so that it includes whoever actually fears and whoever is of such a disposition, as has been said.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 27:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or the heaven?﴾ is an address to those being addressed, in answer to the oath; I mean: you will certainly be resurrected, O people of Makkah who deny the resurrection, on the basis of their claim that it is difficult, by way of rebuke and reproach, after the perfect ease of it in relation to the power of God, exalted is He, has been made clear by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿It will be but one shout,﴾ and ﴿khalqan⁠﻿ (creation)﻿ is put in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) and it is transferred from the subject (mubtada'); that is: is your creation after your death ﴿more difficult⁠﻿﻿ (ashadd)﻿﻿﻿⁠ meaning: harder and more arduous in your estimation? ﴿Or the heaven⁠⁠﻿﻿﻿⁠﻿?⁠﻿﻿ meaning: or the creation of the heaven, despite its greatness and its containing of marvelous wonders at which minds are bewildered when they try to observe even the least of them. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He raised its structure⁠﻿﻿...﻿﻿⁠ etc.⁠﻿﻿ is an explanation and detailing of the manner of its creation, which is understood from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or the heaven.﻿﻿⁠﻿

There is no hidden point in the omission of the agent in this and in the verbs conjoined to it, which draws attention to His being specified and to the magnification of the status of Him, mighty and majestic is He.

And His saying, ﴿He raised its vault﴾, is an explanation of the building: that is, He made the measure of its height above the earth, and its extension toward the direction of elevation, long and lofty. It is also permissible to interpret "samk" (vault/height) as thickness, so the meaning is: He made its thickness elevated in the direction of height. "Samk" is said of thickness because of the elevation of the upper surface above the lower surface; and when this upward extension is considered with respect to the lower part, it is said to have "depth" (ʿumq). A parallel to this is "al-darj" (ascent) and "al-darak" (descent). It has come in sound reports that the height of the lowest heaven above the earth is five hundred years, and the height of each heaven above the one below it, and the thickness of each, is likewise. The apparent meaning is that this is to be measured by ordinary travel, and that the stated number is intended as a determination rather than a multiplication. We follow the apparent meaning, unless some impediment prevents it.

﴿And He leveled it﴾: that is, He made it even in what wisdom requires, so that He, Mighty and Majestic, left no part of it devoid of what wisdom requires for it; and among that is its adornment with the stars. It has also been said: its leveling is making its surface smooth, with no depression or elevation in its surface. It has been said: He made it simple, uniform in its parts and shape, so that some of it is not a plane while some of it is an angle and some of it a line. This is a statement of its true sphericity, and many have gone to it. They said: and al-Imam related it, since it is established that it is originated and in need of a free-choosing agent; so what harm in religion arises from its being spherical? It has also been said: its leveling is completing it with what its perfection is completed by, of stars, complements, epicycles and other things explained in the science of astronomy (al-hay'a), from the saying "sawwa amrahu" (he set his affair right), that is, he put it in order; or from the saying "istawat al-fakihah" (the fruit became ripe) when it ripened. You know that this, together with its being based on the unity of the heavens and the spheres, is not known in the early generation of Muslims, because it did not come from the Companion of the Ascension, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and because no evidence for it appears; and the proofs which the astronomers cite for those matters, their status is not hidden. For this reason, those who oppose them among the astronomers today do not say what it requires. And Allah knows best the reality of the matter.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 29:**

﴿And He made its night dark﴾. That is, He made it dark. It is said: ghatasha al-layl and Allah made it ghatasha (become dark), just as it is said: zalama and azlamahu (he made it dark). It is also said: aghtasha al-layl, just as it is said: adhlama (it became dark). And there occurs: laylah ghatshaa' (a dark night), and layl aghtash and ghatish. al-A'sha said:

"I slaughtered for them my she-camel, making them weak, so their night was pitch-dark and gloomy."

And in al-Bahr, from the book Kitab al-lughat fi al-Qur'an: (aghtasha) means adhlama (made dark) in the dialect of Anmar, and ash'ara (covered).

﴿And He brought forth its forenoon﴾. That is, He made its day manifest. The ḍuḥā (forenoon) in origin, as is understood from the words of al-Raghib, is the spreading of the sun and the extension of the day; then the term was applied to the known time, and it became widespread, and it was used figuratively for the day by way of the contrast (muqabala) indicator. It was also said: the speech is elliptical of a noun (muḍaf); i.e., ḍuḥā of its sun, i.e., the light of its sun, and by this he expressed the day. The first is closer. He expressed the day by the forenoon because it is the most noble and pleasant of its times, and in it there is a revival of spirits that is not in the rest of them, so it was more suitable to the context of reminding the proof to those who deny the resurrection and the return of spirits to their bodies. It was also said: for this reason it was more worthy of mention in the context of favour. The attribution of the night and the forenoon to the sky is because they occur through the setting and rising of the sun, and it is celestial; or, they occur through its motion in its orbit, in it, according to the view that it moves, since it is united with the sphere (falak); or, they occur through the motion of the sun in its orbit, in it, according to the view that the sky and the sphere are distinct, and the moving thing is only the star in the sphere, as the apparent sense of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Each in an orbit they swim﴾ indicates, and the sphere is nothing but the course of the star in the sky. It was also said: they were attributed to it because they are the first things that appear from it; since the beginning of night is by the advance of darkness from the east, and the beginning of day is by the rising of dawn and the advance of light from it. In al-Kashshaf: the night and the sun were attributed to the sky because the night is its shadow, and the sun is the lamp pierced in its atmosphere. It was objected that the night is the shadow of the earth, and it was answered that this is a consideration from the viewpoint of the observer, just as the adornment of the lower sky is also a consideration from the viewpoint of the observer. It was also said: their attribution to it is in regard to the fact that they occur beneath it, and by this consideration it encompasses what hardly occurs to the minds of the Arabs: night and day, each of which lasts six months, and these are night and day at latitude ninety, where the revolution is like a millstone. And it was criticised: they said that the conical shadow of the earth ends at the sphere of Venus, which is in the third heaven, so the restriction is not complete. There is room for consideration in this, so reflect. In sum, the attribution is for the slightest connection.

**[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 30]**

﴿And the earth after that﴾. The apparent meaning is that it refers to what was mentioned earlier: the creation of the heaven, the darkening of the night, and the bringing forth of the day, not the creation of the heaven alone. The accusative of "the earth" (al-ard) is governed by a hidden verb. It has been said that this is in the construction known as *al-shari'a al-tafsir* (the condition of exegesis, in which a verb is implied and then explained by the following clause). It has also been said that its implied verb is: "Remember," "Reflect," or "Mention," and you will know what is in that, God willing.

The meaning of God's words ﴿He spread it out (dahaha)﴾ is that He spread it out and extended it so that its people could dwell in it and move about its regions. It derives from *al-dahw* or *al-dahy*, meaning spreading out. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt's verse supports this:

*And He scattered creatures in it when He spread it out, so they dwell in it until the calling (of the Last Day).*

It has also been said that *dahaha* means "He made it level." They cited the verse of Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl:

*I have submitted my face to the One to whom the earth submits, bearing heavy rocks.*
*He spread it out, and when it was level He fastened it with hands, and set the mountains upon it.*

Most scholars hold the first meaning. The Imam cited Zayd's verse in support of it. The apparent meaning is that its spreading out came after its creation. It has also been said that it was with its creation, so the intended meaning is that it was created already spread out. The first view is narrated from Ibn Abbas, and it removes the apparent contradiction between two verses. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him that a man said to him: "There are two verses in the Book of God which contradict each other." He said: "You have only come to this from your own opinion. Recite." The man recited: ﴿Say: Do you truly disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days?﴾ up to ﴿then He rose to the heaven﴾, and God's words ﴿And the earth after that He spread it out﴾. He said: "God created the earth before He created the heaven, then He created the heaven, then He spread out the earth after He created the heaven. His words, glorified is He, ﴿He spread it out﴾ mean He spread it out."

The Imam objected to this: a great body whose outer surface appears like a level plane, and it is impossible for this great body to be created without its outer surface being spread out and extended. It was answered that perhaps the speaker's meaning of creating it first and spreading it out second is the creation of its matter first, then its composition and its appearance in this form and shape, spread out and extended. This is like what has been said about God's words ﴿Then He rose to the heaven and made them seven heavens﴾: that the heaven's matter was created first, then it was shaped and appeared in its present form. Al-Hasan transmitted something indicating that when the earth was created, before the spreading, it was like a grinding stone (*al-fihr*) and that it was not in its present size. Another scholar objected to this with something else: God's words ﴿He created for you all that is in the earth, then He rose to the heaven﴾, the verse in full. This indicates that the creation of what is in the earth was before the creation of the heavens. It is known that the creation of what is in it came after the spreading out. So how can the spreading out come after the creation of the heavens?

It was answered that *khalaqa* in the verse means "decreed" or "intended to create." It cannot mean actual bringing into existence, because all earthly benefits are continually brought into existence moment by moment. Even if we concede that it means actual bringing into existence, it is possible that it means the creation of their matter in actuality. Some people took *thumma* ("then") to indicate a delay in rank, because the creation of the heaven is more wondrous than the creation of the earth.

Izz al-Din (Isam al-Din) said: "God's words ﴿after that﴾ here are like His words ﴿a brutal, and moreover of doubtful birth﴾. That means: He did to the earth what He did after the heaven had been heard of." The intention is a delay in the reporting. So, according to him, the creation of the earth, its spreading out, the bringing forth of its water and pasture, and the setting of the mountains upon it were before the creation of the heaven, as the apparent sense of the verse in al-Baqara and the apparent sense of the verse in al-Dukhan require. The interpretation of "after" as mentioned above is supported by the fact that taking "after" in its literal sense while taking "that" as referring to the whole of what was mentioned before, which you have heard, entails that the darkening of the night and the bringing forth of the day were before the creation and spreading of the earth. That is not possible if the earth is not created at all, and it is improbable if the earth is created but not great.

Also, it has been said that if "after" does not carry the meaning mentioned, and it is said in a manner similar to what Ibn Abbas said, that the spreading out came after the creation of the heaven, with the creation of the earth preceding without a spreading out upon its creation, the problem of the matter is still not resolved. The verse of al-Dukhan clearly shows that the placing of the firm mountains in the earth was before the creation and leveling of the heaven. This verse, to its end, clearly shows that the placing of the mountains came afterwards. In summary, the exegetes differed as to whether the creation of the heaven precedes the creation of the earth or follows it. Ibn al-Tashkubri said: "Al-Wahidi transmitted from Muqatil that the creation of the heaven precedes the creation of the earth, and a group chose this view. But they said that the creation of what is in the earth comes later. They answered what is here, the verse of al-Baqara, and so on, by saying that *khalaqa* there means decreeing, or means bringing into existence and decreeing the will. They said that the 'after' here refers to the bringing into existence of the earth and all that is in it. As for what is here, and the verse of al-Dukhan, they did the same. They assumed the will in God's words ﴿He created the earth in two days﴾, and likewise in His words, glorified is He, ﴿and He placed in it firm mountains﴾." They said: "What has been mentioned is supported by God's words ﴿Then He said to it and to the earth: Come willingly or unwillingly. They said: We come willingly﴾. The apparent meaning is that *ii'tiya* ('come') refers to coming into existence. If the earth had already existed before, this would not be valid. It is as if He, glorified is He, said: 'Do you truly disbelieve in the One who intended to bring into existence the earth, and what is in it of firm mountains and sustenance, in four days, then turned to the heaven? His will then related to the bringing into existence of the heaven and the earth, and they obeyed the command of creation. So He brought into existence seven heavens in two days, and brought into existence the earth and what is in it in four days.'" The reason the creation of the earth and what is in it appears first in the surahs of al-Baqara and al-Dukhan, before the creation of the heavens, while here it is the reverse, is that the context in the first two is one of bestowing favour and enumerating blessings upon the people of disbelief and of faith. Its requirement is that what is a blessing with respect to the addressees of both groups be mentioned first. So it is as if He, glorified is He, said: "He is the One who arranged your affair before the heaven, then created the heaven." The context here is that of showing the perfection of power, so its requirement is to mention first what is more indicative of it. End of quotation.

In *al-Kashf* it is stated: The exegetes agreed that the creation of the earth and what is in it was completed in four days, then He created the heaven in two days. The exception is what al-Wahidi transmitted in *al-Basit* from Muqatil, that the creation of the heaven precedes the bringing into existence of the earth, let alone its spreading out. The discussion is with the one who distinguishes between bringing into existence and spreading out. As for what has been said, that the spreading out of the earth comes after the creation of the heaven but not after its leveling, it is objected to by saying: "after that" refers to what came before, which is the raising of the height and the leveling. The answer by a delay in rank is not complete in light of what was transmitted about the consensus of the commentators. So the correct view is that *al-ard* is put in the accusative by a hidden verb, such as: "Remember," "Reflect," or "Mention the earth after that." If it is taken as a hidden verb in the construction of exegesis, then "after that" is made a reference to what was mentioned before, the mention of the creation of the heaven, not the creation of the heaven itself. This is to show that it is later in mention than the creation of the heaven, as an indication that it is less clear in indication than the first. It is a completion, as when you say: "Some things, and after that, such and such." This is common in the usage of Arabs and non-Arabs. The reverse is the case when it is used to indicate a delay in rank. *Thumma* may be used in this sense, and so may *fa*. This does not contradict the statement of al-Hasan: that God created the earth at the place of Bayt al-Maqdis, like a grinding stone, with smoke clinging to it. Then He raised the smoke, created the heavens from it, held the grinding stone in its place, and spread out the earth from it. This is God's words ﴿They were joined together, and We split them apart﴾, the verse in full.

This indicates that the heaven being smoke preceded the spreading and leveling of the earth. This is so. Indeed, the apparent meaning of God's words ﴿Then He rose to the heaven, and it was smoke﴾ indicates this. The bringing into existence of the luminous jewel, and looking upon it with the eye of majesty concealed within mercy and beauty, its melting, the distinguishing of its subtle from its dense, the rising of the subtle smoky matter, and the remaining of the dense: all of this preceded the six days. It is established in a sound report, and it does not contradict the verses. As for what al-Wahidi transmitted from Muqatil and the Imam chose, there is no difficulty in it. It is necessarily the case in the surahs of al-Baqara and al-Sajda that the delay is in rank. This is more in accord with the well-known principles of the philosophers. However, it does not agree with what has been transmitted: "God created the body of the earth on Sunday and Monday, spread it out, and created what is in it on Tuesday and Wednesday. He created the heavens and what is in them on Thursday and Friday, and at the end of Friday He created Adam, peace be upon him." End of quotation.

What I incline to is that the leveling of the heaven with what is in it precedes the leveling of the earth with what is in it, because the principle of causation is evident in the upper bodies, and the principle of being caused is evident in the lower bodies. The interpretation of what contradicts this can be known from what you have heard. As for the last report, there is discussion about its soundness. God, Exalted is He, knows best the reality of the matter. Some of what relates to this topic has already passed, and I have repeated the discussion of it only as a reminder to people of understanding. So reflect. God Exalted is the One who grants success in attaining the goal.

Al-Alusi's commentary on Surah al-Nazi'at (79), verse 31:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He brought forth from it its water﴾, by causing springs to gush forth from it and rivers to flow. ﴿And its pasture﴾. The word *al-ra'y* (pasture), with a kasra on the ra', means *al-kala'* (herbage), and *al-ra'y* with a fatha on the ra' is the verbal noun (*al-masdar*). Likewise it applies to the place and to the time. Some have claimed that it is originally for the place, and perhaps he meant that this is its most common meaning. The meaning that suits the context is the first, but it has been said that it is specific to what animals eat, other than humans, and it has been used figuratively for all that is eaten by humans and others. It is therefore a *majaz mursal* (a metonymy, a figurative usage with a non-metaphorical link) of the kind called *al-marsan* (a category of relation in figurative usage).

Al-Tibi said: It may be an explicit metaphor (*isti'ara musarraha*), because the speech is addressed to those who deny the resurrection (*al-hashr*, the gathering for the Last Judgment), as is shown by ﴿Are you a harder creation?﴾. It is as if it were said: O stubborn ones, who are yoked together like the horns of cattle, in enjoying this world and being heedless of the Hereafter. It is an explanation and elaboration of *dahaha* (its spreading out), for settling cannot be achieved merely by spreading and levelling, but there must also be arranging the affairs of livelihood, of food and drink. Or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from its subject, with *qad* implied or not implied, and both views require that the clause be detached from a conjunction (*'atif*).

The verb governing ﴿and the mountains﴾ is an implied verb, which is explained by His words ﴿He set them firm﴾, meaning He fixed them in place. In this there is a reminder that the anchoring (al-rusuww) attributed to the mountains in many passages of the revelation (al-tanzil) is not one of the necessary properties of the mountains themselves. The modern philosophers have made statements about the matter of the earth and how its beginning came about, and they have no basis for them except earthly traces that they claim indicate this, and these are at the lowest part of the earth, far from the realm of acceptance.

Ibn Abi Ablah and Abu al-Sammal read ﴿al-ard﴾ and ﴿al-jibal﴾ in the nominative case. This is, as it is said, on the basis of the nominal sentence (al-ibtida'). Al-Zajjaj criticised it, saying that this is less preferred, because the conjunction would then be with a verbal clause (fi'liyyah). It was objected to him that His words ﴿He built it﴾ explain how the sky was created, and His words ﴿He raised its height﴾ explain the building, whereas the spreading of the earth and what follows it do not enter into any of that. So how can what is conjoined to the whole be conjoined in the manner of one narrative to another narrative? What is taken into account is the harmony between the two narratives, and this is present here, so there is no harm in the difference; indeed there is in it a kind of reminder of this.

It was also said that the clause of His words ﴿and the earth﴾ etc., on both readings, is not conjoined to His words ﴿He raised its height﴾, because it cannot serve as an explanation of the building of the sky. Therefore an antecedent conjunction must be assumed. In that case, on the reading of the majority, a verbal clause is assumed, meaning: He did what He did with the sky; and on the reading of the others, a nominal clause is assumed, meaning: the sky and what is connected with it are created by Him, the Exalted. It was also permitted to conjoin ﴿al-ard﴾ in the nominative to ﴿al-sama'﴾ in terms of meaning, as if it were said: the sky is greater in creation, and the earth after that, meaning: and the earth after what has been mentioned of the sky is greater in creation. Thus it would be parallel to His words ﴿He spread it out﴾ etc., and parallel to His words ﴿He built it﴾ etc. In that case, after that, it does not imply that the spreading of the earth is later than the building of the sky.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 33:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A provision for you and for your cattle﴾, it has been said that it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu, the object of purpose, i.e., the accusative of reason); meaning, He did that as a provision for you and for your cattle, because the benefit of what was mentioned of the spreading out (of the earth), and the bringing forth of water and pasture, reaches them and their cattle. For pasture, as you have heard, is a metaphor for what humans and others eat. It has also been said that it is an infinitive (masdar) emphasizing its implied verb; meaning, He provided for you with that as a provision. Or it is an infinitive not from its own verb, since His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He brings forth from it its water and its pasture﴾ carries the sense of "He provided with that." It has been objected to the first view that the address is to those who deny the resurrection, while the intended purpose is the provisioning of the believers, so it does not fit to make the provisioning of the others like the aim; therefore the latter explanation is preferable. It has been answered that direct address, although specific to those present, has a general ruling, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence, so the outcome is a provisioning of the whole category. Also, the accusative as an infinitive with its implied verb does not remove the objection, since it is a resumption to explain the intended meaning. And it is not hidden that whether the intended meaning is the provisioning of the believers is a matter of debate.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 34:

The saying of Him, glorified is He: ﴿So when the great calamity comes﴾ etc. is a beginning in explaining their return (ma'ad) after explaining the conditions of their livelihood (ma'ash) with His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿as an enjoyment﴾ etc. The fa' (fa) indicates the consequence of what follows upon what precedes, according to what has been said, as the word "enjoyment" (mata') indicates. And al-Tammah (the great calamity) is the greatest of calamities, because it is from tamma, meaning "to rise above," as occurs in the proverb: "The valley flowed and overflowed (fa-tamma) over the villages, and the flood came and overflowed (fa-tamma) the well." Its rising above calamities means its overpowering them, so it returns to what was mentioned before. Therefore, describing it as "the great" is for emphasis. If its being a tammah were explained as its being overpowering to creatures, such that they cannot repel it, then the description would be restrictive. It has been said: its being a tammah is in regard to its overpowering and surpassing the calamities of the world that they knew, and its being "the great" is in regard to its being greater than all calamities absolutely. It has been said other than that. And you know that ﴿al-Tammah al-Kubra﴾ has become like a proper name for the Resurrection. It is also narrated from Ibn Abbas that it is a name among its names here.

From him also, and from al-Hasan, that it is the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thaniyah). Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Qasim ibn al-Walid al-Hamdani that it is the Hour in which the people of Paradise are driven to Paradise and the people of the Fire to the Fire. Both of them also narrated from Amr ibn Qays al-Kindi that it is an hour in which the people of the Fire are driven to the Fire. In the same sense is the saying of Mujahid: it is when they are pushed toward Malik, the keeper of Hell.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 35:

﴿On the day when man will remember what he strove for﴾ is a substitute (badal) of all or part of: "when it comes" (idha ja'at), according to what has been said. It has also been said that it is a substitute of ﴿the Great Calamity﴾, in which case it is in the nominative position, and it takes a fatha because it is attached to a verb, according to the opinion of the Kufans (al-Kufiyyun, the school of grammarians of Kufa). Here the Calamity is the very reality of remembering and manifesting, because the goodness of deeds overcomes every pleasure and anything else overcomes every hardship; likewise, the manifestation of Hellfire, together with being tested by it, overcomes every hardship, and together with being saved from it, overcomes every pleasure. Its artificiality is not hidden. It has also been said that it is an adverbial (zarf) complement of "came" (ja'at), and al-Tabarsi held this view, and he inferred that it is in the accusative governed by "I mean" (a'ni), as an explanation of ﴿the Great Calamity﴾, and that ma is a relative pronoun (mawsulah).

(wa sa'a) means "worked" (amila), and the returning pronoun (al-a'id) is understood; i.e., "for it." The meaning is: on the day when every person remembers what he did of good or evil, by seeing it recorded in his book, which he had forgotten due to extreme heedlessness, or the long passage of time, or the intensity of what he encountered, or its abundance, which makes the one who memorizes unable to retain it, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has recorded it, while they have forgotten it﴾. It is possible that his remembering is by another way. It has also been permitted that ma be a verbal noun (masdariyyah); i.e., he remembers his striving in it.

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, commentary on Surah 79, verse 36:

﴿And Hellfire is made manifest﴾ is conjoined (ʿuṭifa, grammatically coordinated) with ﴿when it comes﴾, and it was said that it is conjoined with ﴿man will remember﴾. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "man", with or without the particle *qad* (indeed) in its estimation, and the relative clause that follows dispenses with the returning pronoun (ʿāʾid, the pronoun linking a relative clause back to its antecedent). Both opinions, as found in *al-Irshad* (Irshad al-ʿAql al-Salim by Abu al-Suʿud), are based on the estimation of the response as ﴿man will remember﴾ or something similar. It will come, God willing, so do not overlook this.

The meaning of *burrizat* ("made manifest") is: it is displayed with a clear manifestation that is hidden from no one, ﴿for whoever sees﴾, whoever he may be. It is related that it will be uncovered, so it blazes, and every person with sight will see it. Some have restricted *min* (the particle in *li-man*, "for whoever") to the disbelievers, but this is nothing.

ʿĀʾisha, Zayd ibn ʿAli, ʿIkrima and Malik ibn Dinar read *wa-barazat* (with the verb in the active voice and without the doubling of the *ra*), and *li-man tara* (with the *tāʾ* on top, i.e. the second person feminine form). On this reading, the pronoun of Hell (Jahannam) is in the verb, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿when it sees them from a distant place﴾. Attributing the seeing to it is figurative (majāz, non-literal usage), whereas it is literal (ḥaqīqa) if God creates that perception in it. It may also be that the address is to the chief of those addressed, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, or to every seer, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿If only you could see when the guilty﴾, meaning: for whoever sees it of the disbelievers.

Abu Nahik, Abu al-Sammal and Harun, on the authority of Abu ʿAmr, read *wa-buriza* (passive voice, without doubling).

[Page 36]

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then as for he who transgressed﴾ and so on, is the response (*jawab*) of *idha* ("when"), taking it as a conditional particle (*shartiyyah*) and not a temporal one (*zarfiyyah*). This is the same construction as in His saying: ﴿And if guidance comes to you from Me﴾ and the verse that follows.

Your saying: "When the Banu Tamim come to you, then as for the disobedient one, humiliate him, and as for the obedient one, honour him." Abu Hayyan preferred this view. It was also said that its response is omitted, as if it were said: "So when it comes, what cannot be described by any attribute occurs." And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Then as for...﴾ and so on, is an elaboration of that omitted response. There is some obscurity in taking it as the response, and it is a sound view. However, there is no obscurity in that once it is established as correct to say: "So when it comes, then indeed the transgressor, the Blazing Fire is his abode, and other than him, in the Garden is his dwelling." The addition of *amma* has only conveyed added emphasis and the confirmation of the sequence and certainty under every interpretation.

It was also said that the response is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, the estimate being: "the deeds became manifest and the scrolls were spread out," or "man remembers what he strove for." Or it is indicated by what follows it, the estimate being: "the beholders divide into two groups." But this is not the right view.

That is, as for he who rebelled and defied obedience, and exceeded the limit in disobedience until he disbelieved.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 38:

﴿Wa-āthara﴾ means "and preferred," i.e., chose ﴿the worldly life﴾, the transient one, which is "on the wing of passing away," so he immersed himself in what he was given to enjoy in it, and did not prepare himself for the eternal life of the Hereafter through faith and obedience.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 39:

﴿Then indeed, the Hellfire﴾ which has been mentioned in its matter, ﴿it is the refuge﴾, that is, its refuge (ma'wahu), according to what the Kufans held, that "al" (the definite article) in such a construction is a substitute (iwad) for the pronominal genitive that was attached to the noun, and through it the connection (al-rabt) is achieved; or the refuge is for him (al-ma'wa lahu), according to the opinion of the Basrans, who count "al" as both a substitute and a connective. This omission here is because it is known that the one who transgressed is the possessor of the refuge, and the ending of the verse with "al-ma'wa" (the refuge) as the closing word (fasilah) made it good; this is the reading that al-Zamakhshari chose. And the pronoun "huwa" (it) is either a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) having no place in i'rab, or it is the pronoun referring to Jahannam as the subject (mubtada'), and the sentence indicates restriction (al-hasr); that is, as if it were said: indeed the Hellfire is his refuge, or a refuge for him, with no refuge for him other than it.

And as for him who feared the standing before his Lord, meaning his standing before the Master of his affair on the Day of the Great Calamity, the Day when man will remember what he strove for. This is on the reading in which the annexation (al-idafa, the grammatical construction of one noun with another) is like that in "ruqud Halab" (the sleeping of Aleppo). Or, it means: "And as for him who feared his Lord, glorified is He," on the reading in which the word ﴿maqam﴾ (standing) is superfluous (muqhamm, inserted without grammatical necessity). In that case the phrase is a kinaya (metonymy) for this meaning and an affirmation of fear of the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, by an eloquent demonstrative method, like what was said about His saying: ﴿Honour his lodging﴾. The full discussion of this has already passed in Surah al-Rahman.

﴿And restrained the soul from desire﴾, meaning he checked and restrained it from destructive desire, which is inclination toward appetites. He disciplined it through patience and by habituating it to preferring good things. He did not attach importance to the goods and splendour of this world, and was not deceived by its adornments and finery, knowing the badness of its final outcome. From Ibn Abbas and Muqatil: it is the man who intends to commit a sin, then remembers his standing before his Lord, glorified is He, for reckoning, so he fears and abandons it. The root meaning of hawa (desire) is simply inclination, but it became common for inclination toward appetite. It was so named, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, because it casts its possessor down (yahwi) in this world into every vain thing, and in the Hereafter into the abyss (al-Hawiyah). For this reason, the one who opposes it is praised. Some of the wise said: "If you want what is right, look at your desire and oppose it."
