Al-Fudayl said: "The best of deeds is opposing desire." Abu Imran al-Mirtili said:

So oppose its desire and disobey it,
for whoever obeys the desire of his soul will be drawn by it into the worst of ends.

And whoever obeys the stubborn soul, it will lead him to ruin,
and cast him into a fall, what a fall!

And so on, beyond that. The ugliness of following desire and the goodness of opposing it have come close to being self-evident, except that those who are free from following it are few. Sahl said: "None is free from desire except the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, and some of the truthful (siddiqin). So blessed is he who is safe from it."

﴿Indeed, Paradise is the refuge﴾ for him, not for anyone else. The apparent meaning is that this distinction is general, applying to the people of the Fire and the people of Paradise.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the two verses were revealed concerning Abu 'Uzayr ibn 'Umayr and his brother Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, may Allah be pleased with him. The first was a tyrant who preferred the worldly life, while Mus'ab feared standing before his Lord and restrained the self from its desires. Mus'ab shielded the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with his own body on the Day of Uhud, when the people scattered from him, until the mashaqis, i.e., the arrows, pierced into his body. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw him writhing in his blood, he said: "I count you with Allah the Exalted (as my reward)." He said to his companions: "I saw him, and he was wearing two garments whose value cannot be known, and the straps of his sandal were of gold." When his brother Abu 'Uzayr was taken captive, his bonds were not tightened out of honour for him. When he was told of this, he said: "He is not a brother to me. Tighten the bonds of your captive, for his mother is the wealthiest of the people of al-Batha' in jewellery and property."

In al-Kashshaf it is stated that he (Abu 'Uzayr) killed his brother Abu 'Aziz on the Day of Uhud. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the two verses were revealed concerning Abu Jahl and Mus'ab. It has been said that the first verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr and his son al-Harith, who were well known for their extremism in disbelief and transgression.

[Page 37]

﴿They ask you about the Hour, "When is its anchoring?"﴾ That is, when is its *irsa'*, meaning its establishing, i.e., when will Allah Most High establish it, bring it into being, and fix it? They mean: when will He set it up, bring it into existence, and make it firm? *Al-Mursa* is a mimi verbal noun (*masdar mimmi*) from *sara* in the sense of "to be firm," and from it comes *al-jibal al-rawasi* ("the firmly set mountains"). The overall meaning of the interrogative clause is a question about the time of its becoming fixed and coming into existence. It is also permissible for *al-mursa* to mean the endpoint, i.e., "when is its terminus and resting place," just as the anchorage of a ship is the place it reaches and comes to rest, so it has been said. Interpreting the interrogative as "when" (*matā*) implies that *al-mursa* is a noun of time (*ism zaman*), whereas his statement "just as..." (*ka-mā anna...*) clearly indicates that it is a noun of place (*ism makan*). For this reason it has been said: the discourse is based on a metaphor (*isti'ara*) that makes the distant day like a traveling person who cannot be reached and cannot be arrived at until he settles in some place; so the apparent meaning has been adopted, as it has been said.

As for the words of the Most High: ﴿As if they, on the day they see it, had not remained but an evening or its morning﴾, it is either a confirmation and emphasis of what the warning (*al-indhar*) implies about the swiftness of the arrival of the thing warned of, especially on the second interpretation. The meaning is: as if, on the day they see it, they had not remained after the warning except a little while. Or it is a response to what they had included in their question, for they used to ask about it in a manner of impatience, hurrying for it, even though it was in the manner of mockery of it (﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾). The meaning is: as if, on the day they see it, they had not remained after the threat of it except for an evening, etc. This discourse, as transmitted from al-Zamakhshari, has a basis, which is: "they had not remained but an hour of a day, its evening or its morning," so this abridged form was placed in its position. The annexation (*idafa*) conveys this meaning, as stated in *al-Kashf*: when you say, "They did not remain but an evening or a morning," it is possible that the evening belongs to one day and the morning to another, so one may imagine continuity from that time to a similar time on the following day. But if you say "its evening or its morning" (*'ashiyyatahu aw duhāhu*), that possibility is not admitted at all. And in your saying "the morning of that evening" there is what suffices in place of your saying "the evening of that day or its morning." Al-Tibi said: it is possible that by "evening" or "morning" is meant the whole day, figuratively; so when it is annexed, it conveys emphasis and negates that possibility, and making it of the type of "I saw him with my own eye" is good. But the earlier interpretation is further from artificiality, and there is no prohibition against combining the two. The fact that the word serves as a closing rhyme (*fāṣila*) also adds to the beauty of the annexation. The residence (*al-labth*) is considered as taking place in this world, while some consider it as taking place in the graves; it is also permissible for it to be in both. *Al-Irshad* chose what we have mentioned earlier and said: what the context requires is to consider its being after the warning or after the threat, in order to confirm the warning and to refute their impatience. The sentence, according to the first interpretation, is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*), as if it were said: "You warn them, resembling in their belief, on the day they see it, one who did not remain after the warning of it except that brief period." According to the second, it is a resumptive sentence (*musta'nafa*) having no place in the grammatical structure (*i'rab*). Moreover, it is not hidden from you that the second interpretation, although good in itself, is not one that comes readily to the understanding; and according to it, it is good to pause on

﴿Fīma﴾ (meaning "About what?"), then it is resumed: ﴿You are not [concerned] with mentioning it﴾, lest it be confused. It has been said that His, exalted is He, saying ﴿Fīma﴾ and so on is connected to their question, as a substitute (badal) for the clause "they ask you...", and so on. Or it is with an implied "saying" (taqdīr al-qawl), meaning: they ask you about the time of the Hour, and they say to you, "In what station are you ﴿with regard to its mention﴾", that is, its knowledge; meaning, "What is the extent of your knowledge of it?" Or they ask you about that, saying to you, "In what station are you...", and so on. And the answer to it [is ...].

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 79, verse 44:

Allah the Exalted's saying: ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾. The weakness of this is not hidden.

Al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) narrated from Aisha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kept asking about the Hour until Allah the Exalted revealed to him: ﴿Why [should] you [be] of mention of it?﴾ ﴿To your Lord is its finality.﴾ So he (ﷺ) ceased, and did not ask about it after that."

Al-Nasa'i and others narrated from Tariq ibn Shihab, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to mention the Hour frequently until this was revealed: ﴿Why [should] you [be] of mention of it?﴾ ﴿To your Lord is its finality.﴾ So he refrained from it."

According to this, it is an expression of wonder at the frequency of his (ﷺ) mention of it, as if it were said: "In what concern and preoccupation are you with mentioning it and asking about it?" The meaning is that they ask you about it, and out of your eagerness to answer them, you keep mentioning it and asking about it. Ibn al-Munayyir objected to this, saying that the Exalted's saying ﴿They ask you﴾ (as if you were concerned with it) indicates that he was at the time of its occurrence settled in it. So reflect.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿Why [should] you [be] of mention of it?﴾ is a denial directed at their question about it; i.e., "In what matter are you [such that you would] mention to them its time and inform them of it, so that they ask you to explain it," like His saying: ﴿They ask you as if you were well-informed about it﴾. So the interrogative is for denial, "fīma" (why/in what) is a predicate placed first, "anta" (you) is a postponed subject, and "min dhikraha" (of mention of it) is with an elided noun, i.e., "mention of its time," related to what the predicate is related to. It has also been said: "fīma" is a denial of their question, and what follows it is a resumptive clause giving the reason for the denial and an explanation of the invalidity of the question; i.e., "Why is this question [asked]?" Then it begins: ﴿You are of mention of it﴾, i.e., your sending, and you are the Seal of the Prophets, sent at the appearance of the Hour, a sign of its signs and an indication that guides them to knowledge of its occurrence in the near future. So for them this level of knowledge is sufficient. Thus the meaning of the Exalted's saying ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾ on this interpretation is that to Him the finality of its knowledge returns, i.e., knowledge of its reality, the details of its matter and the time of its occurrence, not to anyone other than Him, glorified is He. Their duty is only to know of its approach and imminence, and this has been achieved for them through your mission. So what is the point of their asking about it after that?

As for the first interpretation, its meaning is that the finality of knowledge of it belongs to Him, the Mighty and Majestic; none of creation has any share in it, whatever it may be. So why do they ask you about it?

**[Page 38]**

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾. This is a confirmation of what precedes it, His saying: ﴿What [need] have you to mention it?﴾, a clarification of what is meant by it, and an explanation of the duty of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, regarding that matter. The denial that he, may God bless him and grant him peace, should mention any of its [the Hour's] details could, on its apparent meaning, suggest that he, peace and blessings be upon him, has no right to mention it in any way at all. So this is removed by explaining that what is denied of him, may God bless him and grant him peace, is mentioning it to them by specifying its time, as they were asking him about it. The meaning is: You are only a warner to those who fear it and dread its terrors. Your duty is to carry out what you were commanded: to explain its approach and detail the various kinds of terrors within it, as far as you comprehend. You are not one who informs of the specific time of it, which was not entrusted to you. So why do they ask you about what you were not sent for and whose matter was not entrusted to you? On the second interpretation, it is a confirmation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You [are] of its mention﴾, by explaining that his being sent, peace and blessings be upon him, as the Seal of the Prophets, peace be upon them, is a warning of the coming of the Hour, as his saying, may God bless him and grant him peace, expresses: "I and the Hour have been sent like these two, [and] it almost outruns me."

On the first interpretation, the apparent view is that the restriction (qasr) is the restriction of the qualified (mawsuf) to the attribute (sifa). The meaning is: You are nothing but a warner, not one who informs of the time, but one who makes it clear. He mentioned the complement of "warner" only to show that it has a role in the restriction, since the speech concerns a restriction to a specific warner and the negation of a specific informing that is contrasted with it. That it is a restriction of the attribute to the qualified is based on what comes to understanding from the words of al-Sakkaki, that the meaning is: "You are only a warner of the one who fears, not of the one who does not fear; i.e., you are only a warner of those who fear, not others," which suits the context. However, it has been said against this that the phrase "those who fear" (man yakhsha), where "man" is the complement of "warner," is not part of the scope of "innama" at all, so that the final part, to which the warning is restricted, would be the object of restriction. If this were correct, it would entail that what was established above is not correct. But there is dispute over its correctness, since it would also entail that the following would not be correct: "It is only the slave of Zayd, not of 'Amr," and "He is only striking 'Amr, not Zayd," despite the widespread use of such expressions without objection. So reflect.

On the second interpretation, the apparent view is that "innama" is merely for emphasis, adding to the importance given to the matter of the report, and is not for restriction, since no purpose depends on restriction in it according to the apparent meaning, as has been said.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As if they had not remained but an evening or its morning, on the day they see it﴾. This may be a confirmation and emphasis of what the warning implies about how quickly the threatened event will come, especially on the second interpretation. The meaning is: as if, on the day they see it, they had not remained after the warning except for a little while. Or it may be a response to what they embedded in their question. They asked about it in a manner of urging, seeking to hasten it, though in the mode of mockery toward it (﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾). The meaning is: as if, on the day they see it, they had not remained after the threat of it except for an evening or its morning, and so on. This statement, according to what is transmitted from al-Zamakhshari, has a basis, which is: "they did not remain except for an hour of a day, its evening or its morning." So this abridged form was put in its place. The idiomatic construction (idafah) conveys this, as in al-Kashshaf, because if you say, "they did not remain except an evening or a morning (ḍuḥan)," it is possible that the evening belongs to one day and the morning to another, so one would imagine continuation from that time to a similar time on the following day. But if you say "its evening or its morning," this possibility is not admitted at all. And in your saying "the morning of that evening" there is what suffices instead of saying "the evening of that day or its morning." Al-Tibi said: it is possible that by "the evening" or "the morning" is meant the whole day, figuratively. When it is put in the construct form, it conveys emphasis and negates that possibility, and taking it as in the sense of "I saw him with my own eye" is good. But the former is further from forced interpretation, and there is no prohibition against combining the meanings. The fact that the word is a closing rhyme (fasilah) also enhances the construct form. The staying (labth) is considered as occurring in this world by some, and by others as occurring in the graves. It is permitted that it occurs in both. In al-Irshad he preferred what we have mentioned first and said: what the context requires is considering it as occurring after the warning or after the threat, as confirmation of the warning and a rejection of their urging. The clause, on the first interpretation, is a circumstantial clause (ḥal) from the relative pronoun, as if it were said: "you warn them, being likened, on the day they see it, in belief, to one who did not remain after the warning of it except that short period." On the second interpretation it is a resumed clause with no place in the grammatical analysis (i'rab). Nor is it hidden from you that the second interpretation, although good in itself, is something that does not readily come to mind. On it, it is good to pause at ﴿fīma﴾ and then resume with ﴿You are of its mention﴾, lest it be confused. It was also said: the saying of Him, exalted is He, "fīma" and so on, is connected to their question, as an apposition (badal) of the sentence "they ask you..." and so on. Or it is with an implied "saying": that is, "they ask you about the time of the Hour and say to you: in what state are you ﴿of its mention﴾"; that is, of its knowledge: what is the extent of your knowledge of it. Or they ask you about that, saying to you: "in what state are you" and so on. The answer to it is His saying: ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾. The weakness of this is not hidden.

Al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim recorded, and he declared it sound, from Aisha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, kept asking about the Hour until Allah, exalted is He, sent down upon him: ﴿Of what are you in its mention?﴾ ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾. So the Messenger, upon him be peace, ceased, and did not ask after them."

Al-Nasa'i and others recorded from Tariq ibn Shihab, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, used to mention the Hour frequently until there was revealed: ﴿Of what are you in its mention?﴾ ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾, so he refrained from it."

On this basis, the verse is an expression of wonder at the frequency of his, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, mention of it, as if it were said: "in what preoccupation and concern are you with its mention and asking about it?" The meaning is that they ask you about it, and out of your eagerness to answer them you do not cease mentioning it and asking about it. Ibn al-Munayyir objected to this, saying that His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿They ask you as though you were eager about it﴾ refutes it, since the intended meaning is that you do not take pains with asking about it nor are you concerned with it, while they ask you as one who is eager (ḥafiyy) about a thing is asked, that is, one who asks about it much. It was answered that it is possible that he, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, had not, or had not yet, shown eagerness, and then he did; and that their question and the revelation of the verse came after the eagerness had occurred. You know what distance there is in this.

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Khalid al-Hadhdha', Ibn Hurmuz, Isa, Talha, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Muqsim and Abu 'Amr in one narration read "mundhir" (warner) with tanwin and as an active operator (i'mal), and this is the original form of such a word after considering the resemblance (to the verb), and the construct form is for lightness. So it does not conflict with the fact that the original rule for nouns is non-operation, and operation is an accidental result of resemblance. The descriptive when it operates and when it is in construct form for lightness is suitable for the present and the future. When the past is intended, there is only the construct form, as in your saying: "He is the warner of Zayd yesterday." Here it is, according to what was said, for the present, because of its association with "fears" (yakhsha). This does not conflict with the fact that he, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, is a warner in the past and the future, so that it might be said: what suits the state of the message is continuity; and similarly it is permissible in it to operate or not. Then, by "the state" is meant the state of the ruling, not the state of speaking; and on that there is discussion in the books of legal theory, so do not be heedless. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.
